Research on IHL is crucial due to its potential impact on galaxy cluster mass estimates and cosmological constraints. IHL's significance stems from its correlation with the stellar mass of galaxy members and its distribution within the cluster. To address these factors, a new method has been developed to detect IHL through the spatial analysis of stacked galaxy surfaces brightness. The approach involves stacking images of multiple galaxies within a cluster and analyzing the residual surface brightness after subtracting the best-fit model of their collective surface brightness profile. To validate the method, a mock catalog was created to mimic the CIBER survey's sensitivity and resolution. The results demonstrate that IHL can be successfully recovered from the stacked images of galaxies with a signal-to-noise ratio of 10. The Earth observation sector is experiencing rapid growth, thanks to the adoption of cutting-edge technologies such as satellite imaging and mobile LiDAR, as well as the increasing accessibility of large datasets. The integration of advanced machine learning algorithms has significantly enhanced the efficiency and effectiveness of processing these datasets. However, despite these developments, current earth observation platforms still struggle to seamlessly integrate the outputs of these ML models into their core functionalities. In this paper, we introduce EarthNets, a novel framework designed to bridge this gap. By combining the core principles of the Android operating system with ML model management, EarthNets enables the creation of a comprehensive, integrated platform that combines data acquisition, model training, prediction, and visualization capabilities. The benefits of this approach include the empowerment of developers and researchers to deploy ML models on mobile devices, as well as the empowerment of end-users to easily deploy and utilize ML models. We demonstrate the effectiveness of EarthNets through a series of case studies, including the integration of a model for estimating tree height from aerial images. The results show that EarthNets can process the predictions of this model in real-time, leading to a significant increase in the efficiency of the platform. The code and models used in this research will be made available under an open-source license. Our findings suggest that EarthNets can serve as a powerful tool for AI in the context of earth observation, opening up new possibilities for the development of AI-based Earth observation platforms. The first measurement of the polarisation transfer from a target's spin to a proton's spin, as well as between the target and neutron, following the photodisintegration of deuterium at specific energies is presented. The study utilises Polarised Electron Source at High Momentum Spectroscopy Facility and covers energies up to 120 MeV, with polarisation measurements taken by a magneton polarimeter. The findings indicate that, as predicted, the polarisation transfer $C^n_{x'}$ is greater than $C^n_{y'}$, and both $C^n_{x'}$ and $C^n_{y'}$ decrease with increasing energy. Furthermore, the measurements suggest that, at specific energies, the polarisation transfer $C^n_{x'}$ is significantly reduced, potentially indicating the presence of a hexaquark state $d^*(2380)$. This discovery opens up possibilities for future studies, including the examination of other related reactions, and may prompt a re-evaluation of current hexaquark models. Future research could involve the examination of other related reactions, such as $d(e,e'p)$. The study's findings also provide a basis for future investigations into the hexaquark state $d^*(2380)$. The goal of minimax offline reinforcement learning is to develop robust agents that can effectively operate in various environments, even those different from the training data. This paper presents a new approach to assessing the performance of offline reinforcement learning algorithms using historical data. It establishes a general completeness theorem, showing that a wide range of offline reinforcement learning methods can distinguish between sample-based hypotheses and value functions with minimal error. Furthermore, we have demonstrated that a specific offline reinforcement learning algorithm, policy synthesis with value function constraints, can achieve optimal efficiency and accuracy by maximizing action entropy. This enhancement leads to tighter performance bounds and broader applicability compared to previous results, especially in contexts involving high-dimensional actions. Lastly, we have developed a new approach to policy synthesis that can be effectively implemented even in cases where the action dimension is large, relying on gradient descent and adaptive adjustments in the action space. This novel technique is more practical and versatile than existing methods, allowing for improved performance in a wide range of scenarios. Experimental evaluations have confirmed the theoretical guarantees and effectiveness of our approach. For example, it can effectively tackle the complex Atari 2600 benchmarks, which pose significant challenges to other methods, and deliver superior performance in a variety of games, such as Pong and Breakout. This research has significant implications for the design of robust and adaptable agents for real-world applications. altering the facts. To prevent this, we've developed a new approach called FaithfulSum,

$6\%$ improvement. Overall, our research highlights the importance of accurate fact-based 
summarization for applications like fact-checking and source retrieval. The code for 
SummFaithful and FaithfulSum is available at https://github.com/hardik-19/SummFaithful.

The alpha-decay widths and half-lives of superheavy nuclei with atomic numbers 114 to 118 and masses 336 to 352 are calculated using a potential model. These calculations reveal that for certain regions, alpha decay is a primary decay mode, whereas in other cases, the alpha decay or beta delayed alpha decay is the most probable process. Specifically, the alpha decay is found to be hindered in nuclei with a nearly stable two-alpha particle configuration, which undergoes beta delayed alpha decay. To further analyze these findings, the alpha decay widths are evaluated in the context of the Royer and VIVADIS models. Notably, the VIVADIS model yields results that closely match the calculated values. To provide a comprehensive understanding, the alpha decay widths are also compared to experimental data available in the literature. Additionally, the half-lives of these superheavy nuclei are calculated and compared to existing experimental data. It is observed that the calculated half-lives are generally in good agreement with experimental results, with some exceptions. To facilitate further research, the calculated half-lives are tabulated. Finally, the results suggest that the alpha-decay widths are highly sensitive to the neutron-to-proton ratio in the parent nucleus. This observation has implications for the synthesis of superheavy elements via complete fusion in the region of Ds to Rg. Specifically, the calculated data indicate that the decay modes of the parent nucleus should be carefully considered when designing experiments for the synthesis of new superheavy elements. This is particularly relevant for experiments conducted at low bombarding energies, where the decay modes of the parent nucleus can significantly influence the cross-section for the fusion reactions involved in the synthesis process. A detailed examination of the Glauber formalism for describing nucleus-nucleus collisions at high energy and calculating halo nucleus radii is provided. The analysis begins with an in-depth explanation of the Glauber model's underlying principles and mathematical formulation. Subsequently, the Glauber model is extended to account for the effects of nucleon-nucleon shadowing and nucleon-deuteron final state interactions in collisions. Additionally, the impact of nucleon-nucleon interactions in different spin and isospin states is considered. The analysis also investigates how different nuclear density descriptions influence calculated halo nucleus radii and compares theoretical results to experimental data. Notably, the calculated and measured halo radii exhibit a notable discrepancy, which may be attributed to the limitations inherent in the Glauber model. Finally, the study concludes by highlighting the unresolved issues and challenges associated with the Glauber formalism. Deep learning-based segmentation of medical images often exhibits significant variability when applied to new datasets, despite achieving high accuracy on the original training data. This project aims to develop a data-driven method to evaluate and reduce the dependence of a segmenter on the training data, allowing it to perform better on entirely new datasets. We achieve this by analyzing the segmenter's performance on a small set of images from the target dataset and using that information to estimate the segmenter's accuracy on the entire target dataset. Based on this estimation, we selectively apply the segmenter to specific images, rather than using it for every image, to optimize processing efficiency. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach on the 2018 MICCAI BrainTumorSeg dataset and show that it outperforms traditional approaches in terms of accuracy and processing speed. Additionally, our method is adaptable to various types of medical images and can be applied to other tasks, such as classification and detection, with minimal modifications. ITRA enables the extraction of more consistent features from a pre-trained network by aligning its representations at different input locations during the training phase. Lately, applications using augmented reality for mobile devices have been gaining traction, yet the complexity of their requirements demands more than just processing power from devices, making it difficult for a single app to include all necessary features. As a result, developers often use separate apps for different functionalities, which can be inconvenient. Service-based solutions could alleviate this by breaking down complex applications into separate services with their own APIs, but this also requires a more efficient way of composing them. To address this issue, we've developed an enhanced LSTM model that can effectively analyze and decompose AR services, allowing for a seamless and efficient composition process. A crucial component of autonomous navigation systems that utilize visual input is Loop Closure Detection (LCD). Most existing methods rely on memory databases to identify loops, but this approach is hindered by limited storage capacity, high computational requirements, and potential memory corruption. To address these limitations, this study introduces a bi-directional loop closure method that leverages local features to identify loops, thereby reducing the need for external memory. Our novel method achieves real-time performance on mobile devices and boasts a more efficient compression ratio, with no need for additional memory. To validate the effectiveness of this approach, we implemented it within the context of the ORB-SLAM algorithm and tested it using datasets from various environments, including images, videos, and GPS data. Our results demonstrate superior performance capabilities, including real-time processing on mobile devices, reduced memory consumption, and a more compact system design. This research introduces a collection of quantum computer optimizations targeting IBM's Qiskit framework. The optimizations encompass optimizations for quantum circuit construction, circuit synthesis, and compilation as well as decompilation. Specifically, they include a synthesis method for constructing equivalent circuits utilizing fewer qubits, a circuit layout optimization that reduces the number of gates, and decomposition of multi-qubit gates into sequential single-qubit operations. The optimizations are further enhanced with a decompilation method that transforms high-level programming language into equivalent quantum circuit representations, and a circuit translation module that converts the latter into executable Qiskit code. Performance evaluations on actual applications have yielded notable improvements in terms of quantum circuit size, depth, and qubit usage. We've developed a model for strange quark stars by incorporating a density-dependent model into the relativistic mean-field theory, using a quark mass of 150 MeV within the constituent quark model. Our calculations, performed at zero temperature and with a varying pseudoscalar meson mass, demonstrate a positive correlation between the pseudoscalar meson mass and star radius, as well as mass. Furthermore, we have analyzed the dependence of star radius, mass, and tidal deformability on temperature, finding that these properties decrease with temperature and become more rigid in stars. Our calculations also indicate that for temperatures below 0.2 GHz, the star's radius remains nearly constant, whereas it decreases significantly at higher temperatures. Moreover, we have observed that the star's tidal deformability reaches its maximum value at a certain temperature and then declines. Our results align with the LIGO-Virgo collaboration's measurement of the neutron star tidal deformability for a 1.18 solar mass star. Our study suggests that further research is required to fully understand the thermodynamic properties of strange quark stars. Our work may serve as a reference for future research in this area. Additionally, we have made available a Python code for our calculations. For more information, see the GitHub repository at https://github.com/PranavPandian/StrangeStarProperties. In the supplementary material, we have provided a table of our model's parameters and a figure showing the mass-radius relationship for strange stars. Our research investigates how diverse data points impact downstream task performance when learned through specific unsupervised representation techniques. We focus on two techniques: dimensionally-reduced visualization and clustering, and find that the effectiveness of these methods depends on the underlying manifold structure of the data. We discovered that manifolds with a high curvature, both locally and globally, tend to have better outcomes. We quantified these characteristics using the Reiling and Weisfeiler-Zehl-Hopf invariant, and our findings suggest that they play a significant role in determining data point utility for representation tasks. We also propose an approach to identify and remove underperforming training data points, enhancing the overall quality of representations and downstream task performance. GANs have proven to be a powerful tool for creating artificial data, but they face a persistent challenge in training stability due to a phenomenon called mode collapse, which occurs when the model fails to generate diverse samples. In this study, we propose a new approach to detect mode collapse in GANs using the eigenvalues of the Hessian matrix. By analyzing the Hessian eigenvalues, we can identify whether the model is converging or getting stuck in a local minimum. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach by applying it to different GAN architectures and datasets, and show that it can improve mode quality without requiring additional hyperparameter tuning. Additionally, we show that our approach can be used to identify and remove mode collapse in pre-trained GANs. Overall, our study provides a new understanding of mode collapse in GANs and offers a practical method for detecting and preventing it. This paper explores the near-horizon geometry of an asymptotically de Sitter spacetime that is flat at infinity, revealing a key characteristic of the Bianchi IX spacetime family, specifically that it leads to the violation of the strong cosmic censorship conjecture. Our analysis indicates that the apparent horizon gives way to a chaotic, non-compact, and geodesically complete region with positive topological properties, situated between the singularity and the asymptotic region. Notably, this region exhibits a novel feature in which the curvature sign is initially negative, then positive, and then negative again, differing from the Bianchi VIII and IX models. This study presents a cutting-edge hierarchical control system for quadruped robots, combining a location-independent gait controller with a local manipulator controller. The proposed system employs a model-predictive controller to regulate leg movements, ensuring stable foothold locations. By formulating a complex optimization problem, the MPC optimizes overall motion and manipulator control, minimizing the time and workspace spent during the semi-decoupled manipulator task. Experimental validation on the Robust Design of Legged Animal (REALOID) quadruped was successful, yielding a 30% reduction in time spent and an 18% decrease in workspace in the semi-decoupled task, accompanied by a slight increase in workspace in the fully decoupled task. The results demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed system in improving performance over conventional methods. Additionally, the MPC was able to handle dynamic disturbances and changes in manipulator dynamics, ensuring stable and efficient task completion. A video demonstrating the results can be found here: https://youtu.be/4s0qz2JGKQ0. The corresponding code can be accessed at https://github.com/keonlee-m2r/hier-locomanip-control.

The positive-unlabeled learning framework has been a popular choice for addressing classification issues with significant imbalance between positive and unlabeled samples. However, current methods often struggle to maintain stability when training, necessitating the manual adjustment of parameters. Moreover, these approaches typically rely on a positive set that may not be representative of the actual positive class, limiting their effectiveness. To address these limitations, we propose a novel self-supervised positive-unlabeled learning method that employs a robust and efficient training algorithm. This algorithm leverages a contrastive loss to improve the separation between positive and labeled samples, while also utilizing a contrastive loss to refine the positive set. As a result, our approach can effectively capture the true positive class characteristics and achieve superior performance on multiple public datasets, surpassing state-of-the-art methods in this field. Our experiments demonstrate that this method can achieve a significant 5.8% average improvement in AUC. This paper introduces a novel deep learning system for drone detection at various altitudes, consisting of a two-part architecture. It begins with a lightweight neural network capable of efficiently processing video streams in real-time. The network identifies regions of interest and selects the most likely drone sightings within those areas. Subsequently, a second network refines the information and generates a set of key features for each detection. The system's architecture allows for mid-air object tracking, enabling a robot to actively target and follow a drone in real-time while the robot is in pursuit. The proposed method is demonstrated through experiments using a quadcopter and a deep learning model trained on a vast dataset of synthetic images featuring different drone models under various environmental conditions. The results show that the system can accurately identify drones in challenging scenarios and track them in real-time, with impressive performance metrics. In the field of person re-identification, aligning cross-camera images has become a key area of research. Current methods primarily focus on aligning images at the feature level, but ignore the issue of feature discrepancy among images from the same camera. This study introduces a new approach that levels the playing field at the cluster level, allowing each camera's images to be aligned collectively. Theoretical models of Dark Matter often incorporate new particles of relatively low mass, which may manifest as distinct signals at colliders via specific combinations of particles with defined properties. However, these signatures can be complicated by the presence of additional elements like jets, b's, e's, and tau leptons, making it increasingly difficult to pinpoint the relevant signals. To address this challenge, we've developed an approach that relies on machine learning algorithms to isolate the relevant signals from complex scenarios. This method is applied to a hypothetical scenario involving a new fermion, a fermionic Z' boson, and a scalar sunderparticle, all of which coexist and influence one another. By integrating machine learning, we're able to disentangle the relevant signals and accurately reconstruct their properties. The effectiveness of this method is demonstrated through a detailed examination of Dark Matter production processes, and the results are compared to a traditional cut-and-count strategy. This work highlights the potential of machine learning to enhance the reliability of collider searches and discoveries, and the technique may be applied more broadly to a wide range of theoretical models. Ultimately, this research serves as a step towards refining the analysis of complex collider data and uncovering new physics. The associated code is publicly available on GitHub. Deep reinforcement learning algorithms like ensemble Q-learning have been successful in tackling complex problems, but they still face challenges when dealing with large state spaces. One of the primary obstacles is a phenomenon known as value function collapse, which causes the learning process to become stuck in a limited and non-representative space of possible actions. This paper introduces a novel approach to mitigate value function collapse in ensemble Q-learning by integrating a regularization term into the loss function. The proposed method relies on the Fisher Information Matrix to gauge the diversity of representations within the ensembles. Experiment results demonstrate that this approach outperforms traditional methods on the Atari benchmark, yielding improved outcomes in both learning stability and performance. Notably, the effectiveness of this method is validated even in scenarios where the ensembles are trained independently without coordination. This research highlights the significance of representation diversity in ensemble learning and presents a groundbreaking solution to prevent value function collapse. The vast and rapidly expanding world of e-commerce presents significant marketing opportunities for businesses. One key aspect of successful e-commerce page optimization is developing landing pages that not only attract organic search users but also retain them, ultimately driving higher conversion rates. Given the substantial competition in e-commerce, where thousands of pages are vying for attention, it is crucial to design pages that stand out and achieve higher conversion rates. In this paper, we introduce a novel approach to designing e-commerce page layouts using deep learning techniques. Our proposed method utilizes a combination of pre-trained models and a novel loss function to optimize page layout design, resulting in improved conversion rates. Our research demonstrates the effectiveness of this approach in increasing organic search traffic and conversion rates. On a dataset of 1.3 million e-commerce pages with 1.9 million conversion events, we achieved a 0.8% average increase in conversion rates. Furthermore, our results indicate that our method can potentially yield an 8% boost in organic search traffic. Our loss function also outperformed traditional methods by achieving a 0.35% average design change across 40% of page elements. Overall, our research highlights the importance of page layout design in e-commerce and presents a more efficient approach to optimization. The increasing complexity of cyberattacks forces businesses to adopt automated fraud detection methods to safeguard against potential threats. Despite the growing interest in machine learning-based solutions, their vulnerability to malicious attacks has been recognized, prompting the need for effective defense strategies. This study investigates the susceptibility of deep learning models to cyberattacks in the context of tabular data, particularly in the imbalanced data scenario where the minority class requires additional protection. We evaluate the robustness of various neural network architectures, including simple and ensemble models, against two types of adversarial attacks and assess their performance in the minority class. Our findings indicate that ensemble models exhibit greater resilience to malicious attempts compared to simpler approaches. We also highlight the limitations of current attack methods in the imbalanced data context and suggest potential areas for further research. Our research demonstrates the practical application of deep learning models in fraud detection while emphasizing the need for robust and adaptable techniques to ensure their effective deployment in the real world. We introduce a novel graph neural network (GNN) approach, called NODE-SELECT, 
which efficiently processes large-scale graphs by only updating a minimal subset 
of nodes each time. Unlike conventional GNNs, which update the entire node set, 
NODE-SELECT selectively chooses a fraction of nodes (alpha smaller than 1) to 
update, ensuring faster processing and lower computational costs. To identify the 
nodes to be updated, NODE-SELECT employs a k-means clustering algorithm, leveraging 
the node representations from its previous GNN layers. By doing so, NODE-SELECT 
can take advantage of the node representations to determine the nodes most likely 
to be relevant for the task at hand, thus reducing unnecessary node updates. 
Experimental results on the Open Graph Benchmark dataset confirm that NODE-SELECT 
outperforms other GNNs, achieving comparable performance to standard GNNs with 
much reduced computational costs. This demonstrates the potential of NODE-SELECT 
as a promising alternative to conventional GNNs, especially for processing large-scale graphs.

Recent advancements in artificial intelligence have led to the application of reinforcement learning (RL) in game-based scenarios. Notably, RL has been utilized across diverse domains including game development, human behavior, and modeling brain function. This research aims to bridge the gap between game research and neuroscience by introducing a flexible object-oriented task architecture. This architecture draws from the OpenAI Gym framework and provides researchers with a modular system that is easily adaptable across various platforms. Furthermore, this task system is designed to be extensible, accommodating the integration of real-world and simulated environments, as well as the inclusion of multiple learning algorithms. To showcase its extensibility, we have successfully integrated and tested this framework with both simulated and real-world robots, RL models, and several different learning algorithms. Additionally, we have included a practical example of its potential in the field of neuroscience. By integrating the principles of RL, neuroscience, and game development, this task architecture offers a powerful tool for researchers to investigate and model complex behaviors in both artificial and living systems. Its extensible design enables seamless integration of new learning algorithms, sensors, and actuators, ultimately paving the way for groundbreaking discoveries in the field of neuroscience and beyond. Accurate power system planning heavily relies on precise load and generator models derived from a set of representative operating conditions. Traditional methods for creating these models are time-consuming and require a substantial amount of data. In this study, a novel approach utilizing autoencoders is presented to automatically extract a set of representative operating points from extensive power system data. By using autoencoders, it's possible to efficiently reduce the dimensionality of the data and identify the most important features for clustering. The approach also involves using k-means clustering to select a set of optimal operating points. The proposed method was tested on a real-world power system, yielding a set of 100 representative samples that were comparable to those generated by human experts. The results demonstrate the feasibility of this approach in creating high-quality models for power system planning and its potential to significantly reduce the time required for model creation. Furthermore, this technique can be widely applied to other fields requiring dimensionality reduction. The code used in this research is publicly available. The key contributions of this study include the development of a new approach for creating representative operating points, the identification of the most important data features, and the demonstration of the effectiveness of this method in power system planning. The code used in this research is available on GitHub at https://github.com/rraos/representative-operating-points. The results of the experiments are available on the arXiv platform at https://arxiv.org/abs/2306.15017. Future work will involve exploring the use of alternative dimensionality reduction techniques, such as variational autoencoders and deep convolutional autoencoders, as well as incorporating additional data features into the models. The authors are open to collaborating with other researchers to further develop and refine this technique. Market anomalies, such as crashes and sharp rises, can occur unpredictably.
This research aims to categorize market patterns into distinct regimes based on
their propensity for such events. Initially, the paper examines the benefits of
utilizing the optimal transport metric in analyzing market conditions by
demonstrating its effectiveness in identifying and categorizing complex market
behaviors. Subsequently, the authors introduce a novel method for determining
the optimal transport metric by approximating the underlying distribution of
the sampling points using the kernel estimate and proposing a straightforward
approach to calculating the Wasserstein distance in this context. The paper
applies this method to two sets of financial data: daily and intraday stock
market data. Specifically, the authors utilize the daily data to identify
regimes characterized by high and low volatility, while they use the intraday
data to identify regimes marked by high and low trading activity. Ultimately,
the authors employ the proposed method to categorize these regimes and compare
it to alternative methods, including the k-means clustering and the dynamic
factor models, to assess its performance. The findings indicate that the
proposed method is capable of accurately detecting and categorizing complex
regimes in financial markets, offering valuable insights into market trends. 
This study highlights the benefits of the optimal transport metric in analyzing
financial markets and provides a practical guide for practitioners seeking to
apply this metric in their work. The accompanying code can be accessed at the

Classical simulation of quantum circuits is hindered by its memory-intensive 
requirements for wavefunction storage, which is exponential in the circuit's depth. 
A potential solution is to recompile the circuit into a more efficient form that 
consumes less memory - this is analogous to constant-time compilation for circuits 
representing unitary groups. Building on Clifford recompilation, which transforms 
circuit gates into a sequence of controlled-NOT operations, we have developed a 
new method to recompile circuits containing T and S and T* gates, which are 
essential for Shor's algorithm and certain types of error correction. The 
optimised circuits require significantly less storage, a linear amount, and can 
be evaluated in O(L^2) time, compared to the original circuits which require a 
linear amount of time. Furthermore, we have also found a way to reduce the 
computational cost of evaluating the optimized circuits to O(L) time for certain 
types of circuits. This improvement has implications for the simulation of quantum 
circuits that involve multiple levels of parallelization. Additionally, we have 
found a way to simplify the compilation process, which is now comparable to 
constant time, and is independent of the circuit's gates. This is a significant 
advance in the field of classical simulation of quantum circuits. The code for 
this work is available at https://github.com/AndreasKemper/clifford_recompilation.

quantum circuit simulation, and is being carried out in collaboration with the

In a vehicular edge federated learning system, vehicles collaborate to update model parameters by transmitting local data, while a central server optimizes the model. However, highly mobile vehicles create significant delays and limitations due to limited resources, resulting in outdated parameters and limited collaboration. To mitigate this, a new framework, FedMoNet, has been developed, combining mobility awareness and a novel synchronization approach to update model parameters periodically based on vehicle mobility. FedMoNet's design incorporates a new optimization method to determine the ideal update frequency, ensuring vehicles stay connected and collaborate effectively within the system. To further enhance performance, a novel asynchronous aggregation technique has been introduced, which has been integrated into FedMoNet to update model parameters periodically and efficiently. The results of simulations confirm FedMoNet's effectiveness in significantly improving accuracy, with 10% higher vehicle detection rates and 40% fewer data transmissions compared to current systems. Moreover, FedMoNet's adaptability to varying vehicle speeds and different mobility patterns has been demonstrated, showing substantial gains in both accuracy and resource usage. The findings of this research have significant implications for developing efficient and effective vehicular edge learning systems. JADE, a widely used open-source multi-agent platform, has a 20-year history of development and has seen a surge in cloud-based use. However, its original design was not specifically tailored for cloud environments, leading to potential issues such as high memory usage and scalability problems. To address these limitations, a new JADE-based framework has been developed - Persistant And Scalable JADE (PJSADE) - to leverage cloud advantages effectively. PJSADE includes innovative features such as dynamic data allocation, agent migration, load balancing, and data recovery to ensure efficient performance in cloud environments. Performance evaluations were conducted using Real-Time Bidding, a multi-agent system, under both PJSADE and original JADE environments. The results show that PJSADE outperforms JADE in terms of data storage, agent migration, and system scalability, demonstrating its potential as a robust, in-memory, multi-agent platform suitable for cloud applications. The open-source code for PJSADE is publicly available on GitHub under the name "mAFI" at https://github.com/FeiXiao/mAFI. Future research directions involve integrating PJSADE with cloud-based artificial intelligence for multi-agent systems. The sign problem has been a major obstacle to the reliable application of quantum Monte Carlo methods to the strong-coupling regime of field theory. This problem is caused by the complex weights of field configurations under the path integral. Advanced sampling methods, such as the umbrella sampling and bridge sampling algorithms, have been developed to mitigate this issue. However, these methods are not well-suited for use in field theory, where the complex weights are not uniformly distributed. In contrast, the Lefschetz thimble method offers a more suitable approach that can be used to sample the field space along the boundary of a real-valued functional. This paper provides a comprehensive overview of the Lefschetz thimble method and related techniques, such as the extended Lefschetz thimble method and the flow equation method. It also discusses the current status of these methods and their future directions in the context of quantum physics. Specifically, the authors explore the application of these methods to the complex Gross-Neveu model and the Yang-Mills theory, highlighting their potential to facilitate the study of quantum physics in the strong coupling regime. Additionally, the authors discuss the related topics of the flow equation method and the flow-improved path-integral approach. Overall, this paper aims to provide a comprehensive understanding of the Lefschetz thimble method and its applications to the strong coupling regime of quantum physics. Federated learning at scale is rapidly gaining traction due to its ability to enable collaborative training of machine learning models on sensitive data without compromising privacy or integrity.  However, existing federated learning methods are heavily reliant on the assumption that all participants in a model to be trained share identical input data distributions.  This assumption is often violated in real-world scenarios where data distributions across various sites are significantly dissimilar.  In response to this challenge, we introduce a novel, scalable, and privacy-protective framework for federated learning, referred to as MK-FL, which effectively mitigates the impact of differing data distributions on model performance.  MK-FL leverages multiple kernel learning to develop site-specific data distribution representations and adapts these to create unified, global data projections that facilitate information exchange among sites.  Consequently, MK-FL enables each site to independently train models that are tailored to local data and leverage cross-site knowledge to enhance model performance.  Our experimental findings, based on multiple datasets, demonstrate that MK-FL outperforms existing state-of-the-art FL methods in scenarios with significant data distribution disparities.  MK-FL is also designed to be compatible with multiple kernel learning algorithms, offering a versatile framework that can be easily extended to accommodate a broad spectrum of FL approaches. few-shot learning models. Notably, this meta-filter can also be used to refine 
previously trained models, resulting in improved results. When applied without any

In medical imaging, the application of unsupervised domain adaptation (UDA) can significantly enhance performance by leveraging unlabeled target domain data. This paper proposes an innovative UDA model that effectively adapts to target domains through a novel integration of feature disentanglement and graph convolutional networks. By utilizing a generative adversarial network to disentangle target data into target-specific and target-independent features, the model can then utilize a graph neural network to refine target-specific features. Next, the model applies a domain-adaptive graph neural network to align target-specific features with those from the source domain. Finally, the model can utilize these aligned features to achieve superior performance in image classification tasks. Experimentally, the model demonstrates superior performance in comparison to state-of-the-art methods on three benchmark medical image datasets. Notably, the model achieves notable gains in performance on the target domain, with notable improvements in target domain accuracy, domain shift reduction, and domain adaptation scores. For example, the model achieves a significant 3.1% improvement in target domain accuracy on the NIH dataset. Moreover, the model's source-target domain adaptation scores show a substantial 0.6 improvement. Segmenting audio and detecting sound events is a critical task in audio processing.  Current methods, however, are hindered by two main issues.  First, they typically rely on manual annotation of sound events within audio signals, a labor-intensive process that is often time-consuming.  Second, these methods usually employ multi-class classification approaches that are less effective in identifying the precise time frames of sound events.  In an effort to overcome these limitations, we developed the You Only Hear Once algorithm, a novel technique for automatically segmenting audio and detecting sound events. Experimental results demonstrate that YOLO-like models achieve superior performance in audio segmentation and sound event detection tasks, even surpassing human annotators in accuracy.  Additionally, YOLO-like models exhibit state-of-the-art performance in sound event detection tasks, outperforming conventional classification approaches by a significant margin.  The source code and pre-trained models of YOLOV3-Audio will be made publicly available for research and development purposes. A significant obstacle in the design process is coming up with novel ideas, 
which are often better achieved through collaboration between designers and 
non-designers. However, non-professional designers face the challenge of mapping 
their ideas onto actual designs. To address this limitation, we developed an 
algorithm that generates design concepts based on given prompts and visual cues. 
When triggered by an idea from a user, it produces multiple design concepts with 
their respective descriptions. To evaluate the effectiveness of these concepts, we 
conducted a study with 10 participants who assessed the quality, feasibility, and 
viability of the generated designs. Results from our study indicate that users find 
our algorithm-generated designs more original, practical, and feasible than those 
created solely by experts. Furthermore, user feedback suggests that our system 
successfully addresses the design challenge and saves time by automating certain 
aspects of the process. Overall, our algorithm improves the ideation process, 
enables non-professional designers to contribute more effectively, and enhances 
designers' ability to create innovative and sustainable designs. A video 
demonstrating the algorithm's results can be found here: https://youtu.be/4s5qz2s4QsA.

Our results indicate that the proposed method successfully improves navigation efficiency and reduces social collision rates within densely populated environments. Moreover, we found that the addition of the empowerment reward leads to a more natural, distributed pedestrian behavior, which is characterized by reduced social interaction and increased mobility. Our approach is demonstrated in a complex urban environment simulation, where pedestrians are able to coexist and navigate alongside autonomous agents. Our research aims to contribute towards the development of more efficient pedestrian navigation systems, which can also facilitate the creation of more realistic simulated pedestrian behavior for testing and evaluation purposes. This research develops a mathematical model to examine the co-infection dynamics of the current COVID-19 pandemic and influenza-like illness in England. The data used in this study comes from various sources, including the weekly reports from NHS Foundation Trusts and the daily reports from Public Health England. A novel model was created to study the co-infection dynamics, which involved three types of infections: active SARS-CoV-2, active influenza-like illness, and active co-infection in the same individual. The model was developed using a compartmental framework with a set of nonlinear differential equations and was solved using the Euler method. The model parameters were estimated using the nonlinear least squares estimation technique. The results showed that the basic reproduction numbers for the individual infections were 1.89 and 1.21, respectively, and 2.53 for the co-infection. The 95% confidence intervals of the reproduction numbers were estimated to be between 0.88 and 3.01 for SARS-CoV-2, 0.63 and 1.49 for influenza-like illness, and 1.97 and 3.04 for the co-infection. The study found that the total number of infections for influenza-like illness was higher than that of SARS-CoV-2, and the co-infection rate was higher than the individual infection rates. The results also suggest that the total number of co-infections in the population was higher than the individual infection rates. This study highlights the need for a comprehensive approach to epidemic control, where a combined strategy involving both SARS-CoV-2 and influenza-like illness control measures is necessary to effectively manage the current COVID-19 pandemic. The model developed in this study can serve as a useful tool for policymakers to inform their decisions and for researchers to further investigate the co-infection dynamics of SARS-CoV-2 and influenza-like illness. The concept of probabilistic fairness has emerged as an alternative to group fairness in recent years, but its underlying principles are still not well-established. This paper aims to advance the concept of probabilistic fairness by developing a systematic framework for formalizing and implementing it. By drawing inspiration from existing definitions, we propose a comprehensive theory of probabilistic fairness that encompasses key properties and introduces a formal statistical test to validate these properties. Through both theoretical analysis and empirical evaluation, we demonstrate the efficacy of our statistical test and its potential contributions to the field. Specifically, we investigate the potential benefits of probabilistic fairness in the context of educational resource allocation, and our results suggest that probabilistic fairness can provide a more refined and nuanced perspective compared to traditional group fairness approaches. Furthermore, we identify some inherent limitations of probabilistic fairness and outline potential avenues for advancing this line of research. Ultimately, the paper provides a rigorous and systematic foundation for probabilistic fairness, which can serve as a starting point for exploring its applications and contributions to the field. Recent breakthroughs in deep learning-based semantic segmentation have led to the development of several state-of-the-art algorithms, particularly those using the transformer architecture. However, these models face a significant limitation due to their high computational requirements, hindering their practical application in real-world settings. To overcome this challenge, we introduce a novel transformer model designed for efficient semantic segmentation, tailored for use in real-time applications. Our proposed model incorporates a unique self-attention module featuring a spatial attention mask to enhance feature extraction, as well as a lightweight pixel attention module leveraging a cosine similarity function to accelerate computation. By integrating these innovations into a transformer encoder, we create an efficient real-time semantic segmentation model, dubbed RTFormer. Comprehensive evaluations confirm that RTFormer outperforms existing transformer-based models in terms of both performance and computational speed, while also demonstrating its effectiveness in handling complex semantic segmentation tasks. The role of noise in machine learning is a well-established concept, but its nature and characteristics are not yet fully understood. In this study, we propose examining noise through the lens of color theory from set theory, initially testing this concept in the context of deep neural networks classification tasks. Our analysis of the multiclass Perceptual ImageNet dataset using VGG-16 reveals that the colors of the test set, as represented by their RGB values, can effectively predict the classification outcomes of unknown test images. Interestingly, the colors associated with certain neural units exhibit a strong connection to specific semantic classes, while others relate to a broader category of "background" elements. Our findings suggest that color-based representations may serve as a valuable tool for understanding the behavior of deep neural networks and interpreting their internal workings. We discuss potential applications of this method, including its use as a tool for interpretability studies, identifying relationships between different classes, and uncovering patterns within neural networks. Moreover, we propose that this method can be used as a starting point for developing a more comprehensive framework for understanding the behavior of deep neural networks. In the context of grant-free orthogonal frequency division multiple access systems, a non-orthogonal downlink system is proposed where multiple users share the same resource block. This results in an interference problem for the base station, leading to a focus on using advanced machine learning techniques to tackle the successive interference cancellation challenge. Research has demonstrated that deep neural networks can be used to create a near-optimal SIC solution when the transmission power is low. However, when the transmission power is high, a combination of a DNN-based SIC approach and a minimum mean square error combiner is found to approach the optimal result. Moreover, a novel technique is introduced that jointly optimizes the activation function and the number of layers in the DNN, allowing for a more efficient training process. This method is found to outperform the conventional DNN approach in practical scenarios. Additionally, a non-orthogonal uplink system is studied, where the receiver uses a similar deep learning-based SIC approach. Simulation results confirm that this method achieves better performance compared to existing algorithms. Moreover, a hybrid system is proposed, where the hybrid precoding and SIC approaches are combined. This hybrid system is found to offer improved performance and reduced complexity compared to existing schemes. Ultimately, the benefits of this hybrid system are confirmed through simulation results. To the best knowledge of the authors, this is the first work to propose a hybrid system combining deep learning-based SIC and hybrid precoding for non-orthogonal downlink systems. A significant flaw in deep convolutional neural networks (CNNs) is the "dead pixel problem." A single malfunctioning pixel can significantly impair the overall performance of a CNN. This study introduces a new method for detecting this issue, which assesses the impact of individual pixels on network output. Our approach is based on the "effective receptive field," which determines a pixel's influence by measuring the number of times it is visited by the network's receptive field. By analyzing pixel coverage under different network predictions, we can identify which pixels have the most significant impact. Our proposed method achieved an accuracy of 99.99 percent in detecting dead pixels, outperforming existing state-of-the-art solutions. Additionally, we have released a new dataset containing 11,000 images with manually identified dead pixels, consisting of 6000 training images and 2000 validation images, for research purposes. This research introduces AppealNet, a highly-efficient edge/cloud collaborative system that optimizes Deep Neural Networks (DNNs) inference. AppealNet employs an innovative edge/cloud collaborative approach where edge devices and cloud servers work together to achieve balance between efficiency and accuracy. A novel Appeal Mechanism on the edge generates local feature maps and identifies which DNN layers require precise computations from the more powerful cloud server; these layers are then processed by the cloud server, with the remaining less computationally intensive layers executed on the edge. This approach is highly efficient as it minimizes reliance on the cloud, reduces parallel processing requirements, and eliminates the need for additional DNN layers. To achieve optimal performance, AppealNet employs a dynamic scheduling mechanism that determines the most suitable DNN model to run on the edge, given the available hardware constraints. Comprehensive experiments demonstrate the effectiveness of AppealNet, which outperforms existing DNN acceleration methods in terms of accuracy, latency, and energy efficiency. On the ImageNet dataset, AppealNet achieves a 2.4% increase in top-1 accuracy compared to the most accurate DNN acceleration method, while significantly reducing latency and energy consumption. AppealNet also demonstrates superior performance on the COCO dataset, with a 2.2% increase in average precision while achieving a 50% reduction in latency. This research introduces the motion-aware pseudo Siamese network for indoor video head detection in buildings, addressing the need for accurate head detection in surveillance videos from indoor scenarios within buildings. To address this challenge, the study introduces a new approach called motion-aware pseudo Siamese network (MPSN), which combines object detection and optical flow estimation to enhance performance. The MPSN method utilizes a Siamese network to analyze object movement and implement a motion-aware fusion strategy to improve detection accuracy. By integrating this approach with a state-of-the-art object detection model, the study demonstrates the MPSN's effectiveness in achieving superior results on the benchmark dataset, the MOT17 Dev dataset. Experimental results show that MPSN outperforms the baseline model by 8.0% in terms of average precision, 1.1% in terms of average recall, and 1.0% in terms of average false discovery rate. We introduce TIPS, a text-driven generative model that creates a 3D scene's pose representation from a single image as input, accompanied by a brief description of the scene. TIPS generates the pose parameters of a 3D model that are most compatible with the given image and text, outperforming existing methods of its kind. TIPS achieves this by integrating a text-based pose analysis module into a two-stage pose refinement network, leveraging a large dataset of images annotated with both 2D and 3D pose information and text descriptions. The model is evaluated on the COCO dataset and demonstrates superior performance on both 2D and 3D pose detection, as well as on the task of reconstructing 3D scenes using a single image and scene description. We introduce a novel approach to Bayesian mass mapping, leveraging a
trans-dimensional Markov Chain Monte Carlo algorithm to estimate key
parameters, including regularization, noise variance, and intrinsic dimension.
Our model relies on a continuous Dirichlet process prior for the mapping
function, allowing for a non-parametric framework that effectively captures
complex mass density patterns in galaxy clusters.
To enhance convergence, we utilize a modified Metropolis-Hastings proposal,
where the intrinsic dimension parameter is updated via a discrete jump that
determines the number of basis functions in the mapping function, and spatial
locations are updated continuously.
Our approach also incorporates automatic relevance determination for kernel
regression prior, providing a robust and efficient method for mass mapping. 
The trans-dimensional MCMC algorithm ensures robust convergence in all
parameters, eliminating the need for cross-validation to choose the
regularization parameter, as is common in existing methods. 
The proposed approach is successfully demonstrated on simulated and real
data, producing accurate and reliable results. The accompanying code is
available on GitHub at https://github.com/astrolabio/sparsely_bayesian_mass_mapping.

We investigate how novel interactions from exotic particles impact the properties of neutron stars in a specific gravitational theory. These particles are incorporated into neutron star models through modifications to nucleon and many-body dynamics within a generalized gravitational framework. By analyzing the star's equilibrium equations, we determine its tidal deformability and subsequently calculate the star's dimensionless tidal parameters, incorporating various exotic particle combinations. The results show that when these particles have a mass comparable to the nucleon, their presence significantly affects the star's structure, leading to increased tidal parameters, particularly in low-density areas. Conversely, when their mass is much higher, the star's structure is only minimally affected, resulting in a slight increase in tidal parameters, particularly in high-density regions. Notably, when the star's mass is above two solar masses, the presence of exotic fermions can lead to a decrease in tidal parameters, making them more similar to predictions from general relativity. However, when the star's mass is below one solar mass, the presence of these particles results in a slight increase in tidal parameters, making the star's properties more similar to those predicted by alternative gravitational theories. These findings suggest that the incorporation of exotic particles can provide valuable insights into neutron star properties, particularly in alternative gravitational theories. Generative Adversarial Networks have excelled in generating photorealistic images but struggle to produce specific outputs. Researchers have attempted to overcome this limitation by conditioning GANs with labels, segmentations, and other variables. However, these methods are often expensive, unreliable, or difficult to scale. Our study demonstrates that conditioning GANs on latent spaces offers a more efficient and effective approach. By leveraging pre-trained generative networks, we can create high-resolution images from any class, subject to various attributes. Our experiments on the CelebA dataset and the COCO dataset yield impressive results, underscoring the potential of latent space conditioning to unlock a wider range of applications for GANs. Our code is publicly available.

This research introduces a new family of non-parametric statistical tests for determining conditional dependence between random variables, specifically tailored for multivariate Gaussian scenarios. Our method involves dividing the available data samples into smaller, manageable subsets under the assumption of non-rejection, and derives their respective test statistics from local permutation tests for two-variable relationships. These local statistics are then aggregated to produce an overall test result, which provides a reliable measure of the conditional independence hypothesis even when the underlying data does not conform to a Gaussian distribution. Furthermore, we demonstrate that this new approach maintains high statistical power while maintaining robustness, and its practical applications are illustrated through real-world examples. This paper introduces a novel, two-stage approach for restoring images from degraded, noisy data. The method begins by applying nonlocal means filtering to the data, followed by a variational optimization step that can be formulated as a constrained minimization problem involving a combination of data fidelity, regularization, and equality constraints. The overall scheme can be seen as an extension of the classic iterative thresholding method, with the additional constraint ensuring that the restored image retains the original intensity values. Experimental results demonstrate the method's effectiveness in restoring high-contrast images from low-contrast data, with the two-stage approach yielding superior performance over existing noniterative techniques. Furthermore, the method's ability to preserve the original intensity values enables it to accurately identify piecewise constant regions within the restored image. To facilitate reproducibility, the method's source code has been made publicly available on the GitHub repository https://github.com/zhaozheng92/CDCIR. An application of the method to medical imaging is also presented, with the restored image highlighting a tumor region in a patient's liver, based on a T1-weighted MRI sequence. Our findings reveal that these states exhibit singularities in their field-field correlation functions and that these singularities are inherently linked to their entangled characteristics. By applying this method to a simplified model of two interacting particles, we are able to explicitly express the local density matrices in terms of these singularities. Ultimately, we discuss the practical implications of our approach and its potential applications to quantum information science.

Mortality forecasting is particularly demanding due to the significant short-term fluctuations in mortality rates and the long-term trends influenced by factors such as technological advancements and socioeconomic shifts. To address this challenge, a forecasting method using factor models is proposed, which involves decomposing mortality rates into permanent and transitory components. The transitory component accounts for short-term fluctuations, while the permanent component is influenced by time-variant and time-invariant factors. The proposed approach outperforms existing methods on US and European datasets. It demonstrates that time-variant factor loadings are more suitable for short-term forecasting (less than 5 years), whereas time-invariant loadings are more suitable for longer-term forecasting (5 years or more). This method can be applied to any dataset with time series that have strong seasonality and follow a smooth trend. Future directions for expanding this method to other types of data and contexts are discussed. The method's source code is publicly available for download at a specified GitHub repository. This paper outlines a multi-task sequence prediction framework for annotating Tunisian Arabizi, which is a complex morphological task requiring the separation of valid characters from diacritical symbols. By drawing on the nature sequence labeling, the framework models the Arabizi transcription process as a sequence of predictions, encompassing both characters and diacritical symbols. In our approach, a unified transformer encoder is employed to facilitate multi-task prediction, taking in an Arabic text as input and producing two outputs: the annotated text, and a mapping of the original characters to their corresponding diacritical forms. Our framework is trained on paired data consisting of Tunisian Arabizi and its standard Arabic counterparts. To evaluate its performance, we compare it to a single sequence labeling model and a sequential application of character-by-character mapping. Through both automated and manual assessments, we demonstrate the framework's ability to accurately annotate both simple and complex Arabizi forms. Moreover, we highlight the potential for our framework to serve as a training aid for less experienced Arabizi annotators. The implementation details and pre-trained models are available at https://github.com/berkhamlayni/tunisian_arabizi_multi_task. A manual correction dataset is also available at https://github.com/berkhamlayni/tunisian_arabizi_manual_correction. The presented work is part of a larger PhD project focused on the automatic annotation of Tunisian Arabizi. For further information, see https://github.com/berkhamlayni/phd. To facilitate the development of Tunisian Arabizi resources, a new repository has been established at https://github.com/tunisian-arabizi-project/tunisian_arabizi. Our approach employs a two-part framework where an evaluation agent assesses the effectiveness of potential variables at each step, while an action model, guided by a policy, dynamically adjusts the evaluation criteria to maximize performance. We demonstrate the potential of our coarsening scheme through comparative performance analysis against established methods in diverse test cases. Notably, our approach exhibits superior robustness under complex scenarios, outshining competitors, especially in cases featuring singular or nearly singular matrices. Moreover, our criticality function integrates well with existing hybrid Riemann solver algorithms, resulting in improved performance and reduced memory requirements. Ultimately, this research marks a pioneering effort in integrating reinforcement learning into AMG coarsening. All relevant code and data are publicly accessible.

Research has shown that pre-trained language models significantly enhance neural machine translation, yet they are susceptible to semantic discrepancies between source and target texts. This issue is particularly concerning for specialized domains and low-resource languages. To address this, we investigate the effects of semantic divergence on translation and introduce an innovative approach for an unsupervised task-based NMT system. By leveraging a parallel corpus with a semi-automatic alignment procedure, our method incorporates the target language with domain-specific information from a model trained on open-vocabulary data. This approach allows for the effective integration of knowledge and flexibility in adapting to different semantic discrepancies. Experimental results demonstrate that our method outperforms the standard approach in translating low-resource languages and technical domains. Furthermore, our findings indicate that incorporating specialized knowledge is crucial for improving translation quality. Our work provides valuable insights into the impact of semantic discrepancies on NMT systems and offers a practical solution for building NMT systems in low-resource and specialized domains. Recent breakthroughs in machine learning have led to the development of fairer algorithms through representation learning, but the reliability of these models remains uncertain due to the potential for adversarial examples, which can cause harm by appearing to meet fairness standards while still discriminating against protected groups. To address this issue, we introduce a new approach that utilizes dampening and stacking to improve the resilience of fair representation learning to adversarial attacks. Our method incorporates two key components: the addition of a dampening layer that helps to mitigate the effects of adversarial examples, and the use of stacking to combine multiple fair representation models, which can enhance model performance and robustness. Through a thorough evaluation of our approach on various benchmark datasets, we demonstrate its effectiveness in resisting adversarial attacks and achieving superior performance on real-world data. Our results show that the adversarial properties of our method are comparable to or better than those of adversarial training, and our approach outperforms existing state-of-the-art fairness-robustness baselines in terms of both performance and resilience. The next decade in dark energy research will be pivotal due to ongoing and upcoming experiments such as DESI and DESI-like surveys, which will lay the groundwork for a new era of experimentation. Future large-scale experiments like the XENON-1T direct detection findings suggest that breakthroughs are within reach. A new wave of innovative projects will be launched in the mid-2020s, paving the way for a new generation of groundbreaking experiments within the 2025-2035 timeframe. These cutting-edge experiments will significantly impact our understanding of dark energy by providing answers to fundamental questions about the universe's nature and laws. In this white paper, we focus on a crucial aspect of dark energy experiments - addressing systematics in large-scale structure data - and outline a comprehensive plan to tackle this challenge through collaboration and coordination among various projects. This plan is designed to foster a meaningful community-wide effort to address the most pressing systematics challenges and promote a culture of open communication and cooperation among project teams. By working together, we can ensure that future experiments reach their full potential and achieve the desired breakthroughs in dark energy research. Researchers have discovered that large language models possess the ability to recognize and generate meaningful text that is tied to real-world entities, but they struggle to provide clear explanations for their decisions. This limitation makes it challenging to trust these models and ensures that their performance won't deteriorate when they're used in new, out-of-the-ordinary situations. This paper presents an innovative method for evaluating the underlying connection between language models and the world they claim to understand. This evaluation is done by testing the models' ability to apply logical reasoning to the information they've learned. The proposed approach is applied to two tasks: one that requires models to identify and describe the meaning of common place names, and another that requires models to recognize and interpret the meaning of less common entities, such as specific research papers. The results indicate that, although the models can generate answers that seem plausible, the underlying reasoning behind these answers is often flawed. This research demonstrates the importance of developing a reliable way to assess the trustworthiness of language models when they're used to understand the world. Individuals typically organize their activities into scheduled events and less structured time blocks, which we refer to as appointments and blocks, respectively.  Researchers have focused on how people plan their activities in a block format, but there is a lack of understanding regarding how blocks fit into the larger context.  To better understand how people allocate their time, we conducted an analysis using a dataset from Google Calendar that categorizes events and time blocks, and explored how these blocks relate to scheduled appointments.  Our results indicate that blocks are often used in conjunction with appointments and also reveal the importance of considering these blocks in relation to the events that surround them.  By incorporating these blocks into the larger context, we gain insight into how people actually spend their time and are better able to understand the patterns of daily life.  This study highlights the need for further research into the role of time blocks in helping people achieve their goals.  Our analysis also identifies some limitations of the current dataset and provides some potential solutions.  Finally, we outline several future research directions that could help us better understand the role of time blocks in everyday life.  This work was presented at CHI 2020.

A significant concern in the field of cardiovascular disease involves verifying research findings due to a lack of reproducibility. To address this, we developed a framework that utilizes a U-Net to generate a set of synthetic low-dose CT scans, resembling real scans. This allows us to assess whether specific models, including those for calcium scoring, can accurately predict results on artificial data, making them more reliable across various patient populations. By testing these models on a dataset of 1,000 patient scans, we found that our U-Net was able to produce high-quality images that closely aligned with real scans, and subsequent testing on these artificial images revealed consistent results from the models, highlighting their reliability and reproducibility. Furthermore, we found that our framework can be used to simulate various factors, such as different scan settings and patient populations, and our results show that these models can accurately predict results from these artificial data, making them more reliable across various settings. By utilizing this framework, we can better evaluate the reproducibility of research findings in the field of cardiovascular disease. Handling continuous data in classification tasks can be achieved by converting it into a discrete format. This paper presents a novel discretization approach that combines the max-relevance-min-divergence method with the Entropy-based discretization technique. The resulting strategy, called MRMD, is shown to outperform leading discretization methods by significant margins, with improvements ranging from 10 to 45 percent in various classification tasks. When applied to Naive Bayes classification, the proposed MRMD strategy yields outstanding performance on 55 datasets from multiple UCI domains. Furthermore, our results demonstrate that MRMD outperforms other methods on 21 datasets by substantial margins, often exceeding 25 percent. In contrast, Naive Bayes with the MRMD strategy consistently surpasses its competitors, including those employing Support Vector Machines, Decision Trees, and Random Forests, by notable margins. The performance improvements achieved by MRMD are attributed to its ability to balance relevance and divergence while making informed decisions at the local level. The code for this research has been made available on GitHub. GitHub link: https://github.com/Alaairokerk/MaxRelevanceMinDivergence.git. Contact details can be found at kerkrk@gmail.com. The results presented in this study are available on the website https://sites.google.com/amp/page/alaaiokerk.org/datasets. In addition, we have conducted an ablation study to compare the performance of MRMD with other methods, which reveals that the proposed method excels when relevance and divergence are balanced and an informed local approach is taken. The results of this study confirm that MRDM is a reliable discretization method that can be used as a reference standard for future research. The proposed method is also suitable for other machine learning algorithms, including those based on support vectors, trees, and forests. In contrast, the proposed method is not suitable for algorithms that require labeled data for training. The main contributions of this study are the identification of an optimal discretization method, the proposed Max-relevance-min-divergence method, which outperforms other methods by significant margins. Spiking neural networks (SNNs) are gaining attention as energy-efficient alternatives to traditional artificial neural networks (ANNs), thanks to their binary spikes and event-driven architecture. However, SNNs' training process is often complicated by the need for backpropagation, which can be achieved only by approximating the hidden layer's activation function, leading to inaccuracies and difficulties in gradient flow. To address these issues, researchers have developed surrogate gradient methods that approximate the backpropagation process, but these methods are often hindered by high learning instability. This paper investigates the causes of this instability and proposes a novel approach that incorporates regularization and normalization techniques to enhance stability and accuracy for both linear and quadratic surrogate gradient methods. The proposed framework, implemented in the OpenSNN framework, has been successfully tested on various spiking-based learning tasks and outperformed previous results, demonstrating its effectiveness in improving model performance and stability. The framework's open-source availability will facilitate the development of more efficient and accurate SNNs for various applications. This research paper introduces a statistical approach to reconstructing signals from a limited set of measurements, specifically targeting Gaussian mixture distributions. The proposed method leverages the inherent properties of Gaussian mixture distributions to develop an estimator that can accurately identify and differentiate all possible component covariances from the compressed data, even when the number of measurements is equal to or less than the number of signal components. The method involves a two-step process where the first step involves estimating the signal component covariances, and the second step involves calculating the signal component means. The proposed method's accuracy is supported by theoretical bounds on its error and a study that compares its performance to existing techniques. The results show that this method outperforms other methods, such as $\ell_1$ minimization and sparse matrix recovery, when dealing with signals that have a limited number of samples. The proposed method's effectiveness is further demonstrated through experiments involving synthetic and real-world datasets. The findings suggest that this method can provide accurate results even with a small number of measurements, making it a promising solution for signal processing applications. This research presents a novel framework for remote sensing semantic segmentation that combines the principles of active learning, interactive learning, and deep learning techniques. The proposed approach, DIAL, is designed to enhance the performance of semantic segmentation models by identifying and prioritizing the most uncertain samples through an interactive process. The model first utilizes a pre-trained model to segment remote sensing images and then generates uncertainty maps for each category. An iterative interactive process follows, where an active sample is selected from the uncertainty maps and manually annotated by an expert, after which the annotations are incorporated into the model to improve its performance. The performance of the model is evaluated using multiple metrics, including uncertainty maps and the accuracy of the segmentation results. The effectiveness of the DIAL framework is demonstrated through experiments conducted on three distinct datasets, resulting in significant improvements in segmentation accuracy, with gains of up to 15.6% compared to traditional training methods on one of the datasets tested. The DIAL framework is also found to be efficient, requiring only a small fraction of the annotation efforts when utilizing active samples, while achieving substantial performance gains. The performance of the DIAL framework is further compared to other state-of-the-art methods for active and semi-supervised semantic segmentation, with results showing that it is a highly effective approach. The implementation details of the DIAL framework are made publicly available for research purposes. This study highlights the computational requirements necessary for the investigation of dark matter and neutrinos, with a specific focus on the challenges that both fields have in common. To achieve these goals, we propose a multi-faceted approach to computing, including the adoption of cloud computing, in-situ data processing, and innovative software frameworks. Our findings are intended to inform the development of a unified computing strategy for the dark matter and neutrino research communities. Researchers in neural architecture search (NAS) have developed a wide variety of neural network architectures, but the vast number of different models makes it difficult to identify the key characteristics of the most effective networks. To address this limitation, we propose a visual analysis approach that utilizes dimensionality reduction and clustering to identify the most significant patterns in large sets of neural architectures, thereby providing designers with valuable insights and recommendations for creating new, high-performing networks. Our approach has been successfully applied to a popular NAS framework, and the resulting analysis reveals several key insights, including the importance of using residual connections, the effectiveness of large model sizes, and the preference for using the ResNet architecture. We believe that our approach can be easily adapted to a wide range of NAS frameworks, and can provide valuable new insights into the field of neural architecture search.
