In sponsored search markets, the auction system plays a crucial role in determining the most effective bidding and pricing mechanism. To address the challenges faced by Lazada's sponsored search, our proposed system, the Dynamic Reserve Price (DRP) design, aims to increase both user and advertiser value. The DRP design operates on two levels: firstly, the daily reserve price is adjusted based on the previous day's average conversion rate, and secondly, the auction system is enhanced by incorporating a weighted cost-inclusion metric that prioritizes the relevance of ads to avoid low-quality bids. Through experiments using real Lazada data, the DRP design has demonstrated its effectiveness in generating revenue growth rates of up to 5%, while maintaining both user satisfaction and advertiser value within acceptable limits. Furthermore, the DRP design has achieved these results without compromising the overall quality of ads displayed to users. An in-depth analysis of the DRP design's effectiveness also involved simulating ads displayed to users and comparing the DRP design with alternative mechanisms, including a Vickrey-Second Price auction and a Pay Per Click auction with a fixed bid budget. The results show that the DRP design outperforms these alternatives, resulting in higher user and advertiser value. Currently, most studies focus on modeling personalities from dialogue transcripts, but this approach has its limitations. Random feature maps have been widely used to tackle large-scale kernel learning challenges. However, they come with a significant limitation - the size of the feature map grows quadratically with the number of training samples. This severely restricts the number of samples that can be labeled, ultimately compromising model performance. To overcome this hurdle, we introduce a novel meta-learning approach that efficiently learns random feature mappings from limited labeled samples. By leveraging a non-parametric variational random feature model, we derive an unbiased estimate of the target kernel, which we then utilize to guide a meta-learning strategy. This approach enables us to significantly reduce the computational cost of learning feature mappings, making it feasible to handle large, high-dimensional kernels on few and expensively labeled data. Our experiments demonstrate that this method outperforms alternative approaches in few-shot learning tasks across various applications. A conversational agent's effectiveness largely relies on its ability to understand user intentions. In this study, we propose an innovative approach to intent prediction, which leverages examples of specific intents to make more informed decisions. Our method, called "Observers," is a module that collaborates with the primary intent predictor to refine its guesses. The Observer component analyzes a user's input and then passes the results to the primary predictor, which in turn refines its guesses based on the observer's findings. Our experiments demonstrate that the "Observers" module enhances the performance of several established intent prediction models, particularly when they are previously trained on smaller datasets. Observers can be applied to various other tasks and we provide evidence of its adaptability to different datasets and the importance of using high-quality examples when training it. The code for "Observers" is available at this GitHub repository: https://github.com/jacksonhughes/observers. This variant offers a practical solution for agents that have limited training data and allows them to improve their performance with continuous use. We establish that the Langevin Monte Carlo (LMC) algorithm can efficiently produce First-Order Stationary (FOS) solutions for non-log-concave target distributions. Our results apply to a broad class of functions characterized by exponential tails. Specifically, we demonstrate that LMC can generate sequences that converge asymptotically to FOS solutions within O(1/n) distance from the true FOS solution with high probability. Our research builds on recent advances in non-asymptotic sampling analysis and provides a more comprehensive understanding of non-log-concave sampling theory. We also demonstrate the practical utility of our results through numerical experiments. In particular, we show that LMC can effectively produce high-quality samples for non-log-concave distributions in applications involving Bayesian optimization and feature selection tasks. Furthermore, our results indicate that LMC outperforms other sampling algorithms, including the Random Walk (RW) and Metropolis-Hastings (MH) algorithms, in these scenarios. We also observe that LMC produces high-quality solutions in a significant proportion of cases, although the algorithm may occasionally fall short in finding optimal solutions for more complex function spaces. Overall, our research provides a more comprehensive understanding of non-log-concave sampling and demonstrates the effectiveness of LMC in solving a range of practical problems. The key contributions of our paper include the establishment of new non-asymptotic guarantees for LMC, the development of a new theory for non-log-concave sampling, and the demonstration of the algorithm's practical utility in real-world applications. We believe that our research will inspire further advances in sampling analysis and efficient optimization algorithms. Additionally, our results provide a new perspective on the effectiveness of LMC in solving complex optimization tasks. In League of Legends, a popular multiplayer online battle arena game, players can select their champions for each match. Different champions possess distinct abilities, rendering some champions more suitable for specific match outcomes than others. To determine the most probable outcome of a match, we analyze the champion compositions of the opposing teams, leveraging this information to make informed predictions. Our study focuses on the top 30 most frequently played champions in the 2019 World Championship, represented by both their summoner names and player IDs. Our findings also suggest that champion experience is a highly effective predictor of match outcomes, and that further investigation into other relevant features, such as team statistics and item usage, may enhance the accuracy of our models. This research introduces a novel method for disentangling representations using a semi-supervised approach grounded in Generative Adversarial Networks. Our approach leverages the capabilities of the StyleGAN-4 model to produce a vast array of photorealistic images, while training the latent space to separate individual components of an image into distinct latent vectors for each characteristic. This technique enables a single image to be decomposed into and reassembled from independent latent vectors. Our method has been successfully applied to disentangle representations of images captured using multiple modalities such as infrared, thermal, and RGB images. Our results indicate that the semi-supervised disentanglement approach outperforms other methods, even when limited to only a small dataset size, requiring minimal annotated infrared-thermal images. This research has significant implications for the development of advanced image-based applications for autonomous vehicles and military operations in the dark and adversarial environments. Highly detailed hyperspectral images are crucial for a variety of applications, 
but they're often limited by low signal quality.  The addition of a highly 
noisy sensor further exacerbates the issue.  Traditional methods for cleaning 
these images have focused on individual pixels, which can't capture relationships 
between nearby pixels.  In an attempt to address this, a new approach called 
SSCAN has been developed, which combines cross-attention techniques with 
deep learning.  SSCAN first separates hyperspectral images into distinct groups 
of neighboring pixels, then uses a unique attention-based system to analyze 
spectral patterns and spatial relationships.  The approach leverages this analysis 
to create a highly accurate, noise-free hyperspectral image.  The results of 
SSCAN have outperformed existing methods in several key areas, including PSNR, 
SSIM, and the number of preserved details.  The approach has also demonstrated 
its ability to handle images with complex patterns and diverse noise levels.  The 
source code will be made available for public use.  We anticipate that SSCAN will 
play a significant role in advancing the field of hyperspectral imaging and its

The findings presented here generalize a previously established result concerning representations of Lie algebras. Additionally, an illustrative example is provided to support the conclusions made. Under the assumption that a Bol algebra possesses a center of zero characteristic, specific subcategories of linear and symmetric tensor representations are identified and shown to be isomorphic to each other. The final section of this research paper describes a process to obtain a representation that is invariant to any given linear transformation of a Bol algebra. The findings presented here also apply to a broader range of nonassociative algebras. In multi-agent reinforcement learning, the challenge of learning in groups persists.  A widely accepted notion is that agents must collaborate to form a single team. However, in real-world scenarios, cooperation is not always feasible and agents may need to work independently. This paper addresses this issue by introducing the concept of independent learning in multi-agent reinforcement learning. We propose the 'Satisficing Path' as a solution to achieve stable, high-reward outcomes in independent learning environments. We also develop a learning algorithm, 'Independent Satisficing Paths', which adapts to these environments by encouraging agents to explore their own paths to high rewards while minimizing interference from one another. Our results show that this approach outperforms existing methods in challenging multi-agent reinforcement learning scenarios. A novel method called Spatial Assembly is introduced, enabling the creation of intricate, three-dimensional structures composed of numerous objects. Employing reinforcement learning, this algorithm optimizes the position, orientation, and composition of these objects. Based on a novel spatial representation, Spatial Assembly is capable of learning from self-play and utilizing a tree search for added benefits. Experimental comparisons reveal that Spatial Assembly produces higher-quality, self-similar structures compared to other approaches. Furthermore, this algorithm is demonstrated to be superior to other spatial and RL methods in various applications, including designing stable towers, creating efficient planar packing systems, and crafting rationally designed molecular structures. As a result, Spatial Assembly is poised to contribute significantly to advancements in fields like architecture, materials science, and drug development. Conventional self-supervised learning methods often utilize a large, balanced dataset to train, but researchers encounter an issue when working with real-world datasets that are imbalanced due to underrepresentation of certain classes. The resulting class bias affects the performance of the models, limiting their ability to generalize across classes. To overcome this challenge, we investigate the impact of imbalanced datasets on different self-supervised learning methods and introduce a straightforward technique to enhance the resilience of these models against class bias. The proposed approach involves training the model using a balanced dataset and then conducting a series of simulations using the imbalanced dataset, employing a class-shifting transformation to test the model's ability to adapt and maintain its performance across classes. Our results indicate that the imbalanced dataset simulation technique effectively evaluates a model's ability to generalize and detect class bias. By comparing the robustness of various self-supervised learning methods, we demonstrate that two specific approaches, SimSiam and BYOL, exhibit superior performance and can be modified to achieve greater robustness against class bias. The proposed techniques can be easily integrated into existing self-supervised learning methods to enhance their ability to generalize across classes and manage class bias. We investigate the scenario where multiple parties collaborate to calculate a model using private data, while a malicious party could disrupt the process by manipulating the data provided. Our proposed solution employs linearly separable models, which can effectively minimize data exposure, thus enhancing security. Our proposed solution outperforms existing work in terms of both security and data utility. Furthermore, simulation results indicate that the system's robustness is highly effective against various types of corruption, thus further enhancing its practical applicability. We analyze the behavior of continuous-time non-autonomous weakly interacting particle systems in d-dimensional space, considering both attractive and repulsive interactions. When interactions are repulsive and particles are initially spaced far enough, we demonstrate that the particle system converges weakly to a non-autonomous Ornstein-Uhlenbeck process, with no requirement for the interaction function to be locally bounded. Conversely, with attractive interactions, we show that the particle system almost certainly experiences collapse if its initial configuration exceeds a critical density, whereas if its density is below this threshold, the particles remain separated and form a unique limit that differs from the Ornstein-Uhlenbeck process, representing a distinct type of random motion. This research generalizes earlier findings for finite systems to a continuous context, with a non-autonomous setting being a new area of investigation. We then introduce a new measure of stability that aligns with this revised framework and validate its effectiveness through both theoretical and empirical analysis. Ultimately, our work provides a foundation for rethinking the importance of stability in attribution-based explanations and highlights the need for more robust and accurate methods. This paper introduces an efficient, real-time trajectory smoothing approach that 
processes smoothing data in real-time for complex trajectories in motion planning 
applications. It leverages a stateless convolutional neural network to generate 
smooth paths from raw motion data. Our innovative use of the separable convolution 
inference method enables real-time processing at 100 Hz for complex trajectories. 
Comparative studies reveal our method surpass existing alternatives in terms of 
real-time performance by approximately 4-5 times without compromising smoothing quality. 
Notably, it outperforms a leading approach in terms of smoothing quality, achieving 
smoothness scores 23% higher. Our method's exceptional real-time performance makes 
it suitable for applications requiring fast trajectory smoothing, such as autonomous vehicles.

The Local Hamiltonian Problem (LHP) is a critical issue within quantum computing research.  A variant of the problem, LHP-Parity, has been studied, where the task is to locate a qubit configuration in a many-qubit system that yields a product state with an energy that falls within pre-specified bounds. In this research, we investigate the optimal distribution of social connections to effectively counterbalance prevailing opinions in a social network. Our model accounts for a phenomenon known as the backfire effect, where individuals become more entrenched in their thoughts when confronted with opposing views. We formulate an optimal depolarisation strategy within a specific class of social networks and derive a mathematical formula for determining the most effective exposure to opposing opinions. Our findings indicate that the optimal strategy often diverges from equal exposure to all connections, with a specified ratio of adverse connections required to achieve optimal results. When the backfire effect is absent, this ratio approximates the total number of adverse connections. We also find that the optimal strategy is influenced by network structure, with larger networks and diverse connections contributing to more effective counterbalancing. Finally, we explore the practical implications of our research, discussing potential limitations and directions for future work. The rapid advancements in technology have led to the widespread adoption of mobile devices like GPS trackers and smartphones that provide detailed data on user locations. This data is highly valuable for various applications, such as optimizing routes and scheduling tasks, as well as for predicting and optimizing public transportation systems. This research focuses on leveraging data from mobile devices to predict changes in bus frequency in real-time. The study first presents a dataset of bus routes in Warsaw, Poland, collected from GPS-equipped vehicles and mobile devices via a Wi-Fi based system. The data is then analyzed using machine learning methods to identify key patterns and predictors of changes in bus frequency. The study finds that the time of day, number of active devices within a bus's coverage area, and distance traveled by the bus are significant factors influencing bus frequency. The research demonstrates the effectiveness of our approach by comparing it with other methods and achieving promising results. The findings have the potential to be applied in real-world settings, contributing to more efficient and optimized public transportation systems. To improve video conferencing quality, we have developed Gemino, an innovative neural compression codec that significantly reduces encoding and decoding delays. Unlike conventional methods that sacrifice quality for speed, Gemino enables fast video transmission with minimal impact on visual clarity. Our approach leverages a novel hybrid codec that incorporates a powerful end-to-end learned video encoder, a highly efficient quantization module, and a low-latency video decoder. By integrating these tools, Gemino efficiently processes high-quality video frames in real-time, outperforming current standards. Our experiments demonstrate Gemino's effectiveness on real-world video conferencing datasets, resulting in substantial improvements in PSNR and MS-SSIM quality, with a 2x-8x reduction in end-to-end encoding and decoding time compared to industry standards. Additionally, Gemino's robustness to packet loss and encoding rate variability was confirmed through extensive simulations of real-world network errors. We introduce Cloth Funnels, a versatile and efficient method for simulating a range of garment handling tasks, such as donning, dressing, and reconfiguring garments on virtual figures. Our approach leverages a recently developed, adaptive cloth model, which simplifies the simulation process while maintaining physical accuracy. By transforming the complex process of garment manipulation into a flow of particles within a dynamic framework, our method effectively reduces the computational complexity. Additionally, we present a novel technique for measuring and aligning garment fibers that enhances the overall performance and generalizability of our system. Through extensive evaluations, we demonstrate that our method surpasses state-of-the-art approaches in terms of both performance and versatility. Our framework achieves a significant speedup, achieving 20 times greater efficiency than previous state-of-the-art methods. We also showcase its potential in real-world applications through a demonstration of its ability to generate realistic, multi-step animations of garment manipulation tasks. We investigate the distribution of galactic clusters in a modified gravity theory known as Finzi gravity, where a small correction term is added to Newton's gravitational force in the large distance limit. Using a theoretical model, we derive the probability distribution of galactic clusters as a function of their gravitational influence, and then test this model against observational data to determine the best-fit parameters. Our analysis reveals that incorporating this modification into Finzi gravity results in a more accurate fit to the data, and yields estimates for the characteristic scale and mass of galactic clusters. We also examine the relationship between this model and the established Poisson process model, and discuss the implications of our findings for the understanding of galaxy and galaxy cluster formation. However, current methods often struggle to effectively model relationships between Chinese video content and text data. To overcome this limitation, we introduce a novel pre-training approach that leverages a large, diverse dataset of Chinese video and text pairs to learn multimodal representations. the limitations of this method become apparent when dealing with scenarios where 
small perturbations lead to significant non-linear responses in the system. In such 
cases, second-order sensitivity analysis emerges as a promising direction for 
further improvement. In this context, we develop a framework to compute second-order 
sensitivity values in bilevel optimization problems and demonstrate its 
efficiency in addressing the aforementioned limitations. The proposed approach 
is validated by its successful application in designing a high-precision control 
controller. The corresponding MATLAB code is made publicly available for 
research purposes. Through numerical simulations, we showcase the superiority of 
this method over traditional first-order analysis in achieving more accurate 
results. Additionally, we provide a comprehensive comparison of the computational 
efficiency of the two approaches. Finally, we showcase the practical application 
of this method in real-world engineering control systems. The results indicate that 
the proposed controller exhibits enhanced performance compared to existing methods. 
Moreover, the computational complexity of the proposed approach is found to be lower, 
especially when dealing with large systems. The potential applications of this method 
extend beyond control systems, making it a valuable tool for addressing various 
optimization challenges. The implementation of the proposed approach is also demonstrated.

The primary objective of salient object detection is to identify the most visually prominent objects within images. Current methods heavily rely on extensive, pixel-level annotations for this task. In this research, we propose a novel weakly-supervised approach, referred to as weakly-supervised subitizing, which significantly reduces the need for annotations. By leveraging the subitizing phenomenon, where humans can accurately identify up to three objects, we can train our model using limited, categorical labels instead of precise, pixel-level segmentations. To verify the effectiveness of our proposed method, we have developed a new, weakly-supervised dataset called Subitizing-1000, which includes categorical labels for up to three objects per image. Our comprehensive evaluation of subitizing-based approaches on this new dataset demonstrates substantial improvements over current state-of-the-art methods when using the same limited number of annotations. The results of our experiments also confirm that subitizing-based approaches are particularly beneficial when there is a shortage of available annotations. Furthermore, we provide a comprehensive ablation study to validate the effectiveness of ViT-BEVSeg. To facilitate research, we have made our code and models publicly available on GitHub. Open-set recognition is a challenging task in its own right, and when applied to object detection, it requires identifying objects that don't belong to training classes. Current approaches to open-set detection either rely on closed-set classifiers or use synthetic negative examples. However, these methods have limitations: they either sacrifice detection performance for open-set robustness or need extra data and computational resources. In response, we propose a new framework, SAL-OD, that leverages the training data to enhance its performance on both closed and open sets. By incorporating an auxiliary loss function, SAL-OD refines its detector to avoid misidentifying unknown objects as known ones. This approach eliminates the need for additional data and enhances detection accuracy in open sets, outperforming existing methods. SAL-OD has been successfully tested on COCO and MSCOCO datasets under various conditions, and its code has been made publicly available. In particular, it has achieved state-of-the-art results on these datasets when using synthetic data, and comparable results to top-performing methods on real unknown data.
